clue.text: Straggle headed by elderly goose

indicators.note: What is headed by something has that thing at its top, so the word named after it is written in front.

parts.note: hair goes grey with age, so elderly reads as the colour
to straggle along behind is to lag

explanation.surface: A straggling line of walkers with an old goose leading them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Headed by' is the only instruction in the sentence, and it settles the running order rather than describing a bird at the front. Grey stands for elderly by way of hair, not weather.
explanation.definitionFit: The greylag is the large grey wild goose of northern Europe, the bird every farmyard goose is descended from.

clue.text: Indian sides in garnish finish off tandoori

parts.note: the two sides of the word garnish are its outer letters G and H, so the phrase reads literally as 'G and H'

indicators.note: the finish of a word is its last letter, so this picks the end of tandoori

parts.note: its final letter is I

explanation.surface: A cook is told to garnish the side dishes and finish off the tandoori for an Indian meal.
explanation.walkthrough: The sides of 'garnish' are G and H, and the clue wants the full phrase 'G and H' spelt out as letters; 'finish off' then adds the last letter of tandoori.
explanation.definitionFit: Mahatma Gandhi, leader of the independence movement, is the most famous Indian figure of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Occasionally gearbox can be mounted again

definitions.note: The answer is a noun in English, but the shout itself is the French for 'again', which is the sense the single word defines.

indicators.note: What happens occasionally happens at intervals rather than every time, so only every second letter is taken.
Something mounted has been carried upwards, and in a down entry that means the letters are read back up the grid.

parts.note: every second letter of gEaRbOx CaN bE, before it is stood the other way up

explanation.surface: A gearbox picked out of the scrapyard and fitted once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can be' looks like ordinary grammar holding the sentence together and is half the letter supply. The definition is the last word on its own, doing no scene-setting at all.
explanation.definitionFit: An encore is the extra number played when the audience wants the music again, and the word is simply French for 'again'.

clue.text: Explosive change I implement

indicators.note: Change something and it no longer looks as it did, so the letters beside this come out in a different order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: Someone announcing a drastic change they are about to put into effect.
explanation.walkthrough: The pronoun pulls its weight: without the I there are only nine letters. A limpet mine is the magnetic charge a diver clamps to a hull, named for the shellfish that grips a rock.
explanation.definitionFit: A limpet mine is a charge stuck to a ship's side and timed to blow, so 'explosive' is the noun in its plainest sense.

clue.text: Fix up label or it might snap

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' says the word fixed on is written from the bottom upwards, so label's synonym is read backwards

parts.note: a label is a tag
taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to stick a label on something, with a warning that it might snap shut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fix up' writes TAG, the word for label, upwards in this down clue to give GAT, then OR follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A gator, short for alligator, is a reptile whose powerful jaws snap shut on prey.

clue.text: Parents postponing employment of second hot water bottle?

indicators.note: To postpone something is to put it back until later, so the piece named next is held over until further along the word.

parts.note: parents are mothers, and with the MO lifted off the front THERS is what remains
a mo is a second, put back to work later in the word

explanation.surface: Parents putting off buying a second hot water bottle for the bed.
explanation.walkthrough: A hot water bottle is the rubber one in the bed everywhere except here, where the three words are meant literally: a bottle that holds hot water. 'Second' is the moment, not the ordinal.
explanation.definitionFit: A thermos is a vacuum flask, and what it is carried for is keeping water hot, so the three words describe it exactly.

clue.text: Stabbing item about to corrode

indicators.note: A thing set about something is wrapped round it, so the word just named closes over the one that follows.

parts.note: an item is a thing
iron left out to corrode will rust

explanation.surface: A blade in the shed that is on the point of going rusty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to corrode' reads as one phrase meaning nearly rusty and splits into an instruction plus a word. The definition is the motion, a thrusting blow, rather than a thing that stabs.
explanation.definitionFit: To thrust is to drive a blade home, so stabbing and thrusting name the same jabbing movement.

clue.text: Going through hairpieces, a usually hairy chap

indicators.note: What goes through a thing runs inside it from one end to the other, so the answer lies straight across the words that follow.

parts.note: the letters run on through hairpiecES, A Usually

explanation.surface: Someone rummaging through a box of wigs for a notably hairy man.
explanation.walkthrough: Esau is the hairy twin of Genesis, who sold his birthright to smooth-skinned Jacob for a bowl of stew. 'Usually' looks like padding and is carrying the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Esau was born covered in red hair, which is the detail Genesis uses to tell him from his smooth brother, so the description is him exactly.

clue.text: Material holding up Piers, a lot of type?

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits above the second and holds it up

parts.note: a mole is a pier or breakwater, so piers are moles

indicators.note: most of the word, so its final letter is dropped

explanation.walkthrough: A mole is a stone breakwater; 'a lot of' trims KIND (type) to KIN, and 'holding up' puts MOLES above it in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Moleskin is a heavy cotton fabric with a soft brushed surface, used for trousers and jackets.

clue.text: Second politician, rejecting leader, left

indicators.note: the politician loses the first letter of the word

explanation.walkthrough: 'rejecting leader' removes the first letter M from MINISTER, leaving INISTER after S.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinister is the heraldic and Latin term for the left-hand side.

clue.text: Computer at home backing up sound system

indicators.note: Something backing up is travelling in reverse, so the letters just named are read from their far end.

parts.note: the Mac is Apple's computer, short for Macintosh
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: Someone at home backing up their computer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing up' is the household chore in the sentence and the turnaround in the grid. NICAM is the digital stereo standard British broadcasters have carried television sound on since the late eighties.
explanation.definitionFit: NICAM is the two-channel digital sound British television is transmitted with, so the answer is a system for sound rather than a hi-fi in the corner.

clue.text: This provides cover until para breaks out

indicators.note: Something that breaks out bursts its bounds and scatters, so the letters beside this are set down in a new order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Something a paratrooper shelters under until the moment he bursts out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaks out' reads as the soldier making his move and is the instruction; the two words before it are nothing but letters. The word is tarred palling, cloth waterproofed with tar.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarpaulin is the waterproof sheet thrown over whatever has to stay dry, so it is a cover in the literal sense.

clue.text: Rough-spoken insolence that groom must polish up?

definitions.note: The definition describes the answer rather than replacing it: 'that' stands for the object itself, named by whose job it is to keep it shining.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish up' is the manners lesson in the sentence and literal buffing in the answer: horse brasses are the shining medallions hung on a heavy horse's harness, and keeping them bright falls to whoever looks after the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse brass is the round polished ornament fixed to a cart-horse's harness, and the groom is the one who rubs it up.

clue.text: Sierra tailgates Clio maybe out of motorway services

indicators.note: A car that tailgates sits right on the tail of the one in front, so this letter goes behind what the rest of the wordplay builds.
Taken out of a word, the letters named next are removed from it.

Sierra is S in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: A Sierra sitting on a Clio's bumper coming out of the motorway services.
explanation.walkthrough: Three cars and a road keep the surface moving, but the Clio wanted is the Muse of history. 'Services' is the roadside stop in the picture and a plain plural noun in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A thing's services are the uses it is put to, as when something is pressed into service, so the two plural nouns swap cleanly.

clue.text: Formal outdoor feature that could spell danger for setter?

definitions.meaning: read straight: the Tudor arrangement of low clipped box hedges laid out in interlacing patterns

definitions.text: that could spell danger for setter?
definitions.meaning: read as a hazard lurking in the grounds, and meant as wordplay a setter could write, the first word being an order to tangle and the second the six letters that come out as DANGER

explanation.surface: A formal garden with some hazard in it for whoever laid it out.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters clue DANGER as a shuffle of GARDEN all the time; here the answer is that clue, indicator and all, which is why nothing in the sentence hands any letters over.
explanation.definitionFit: A knot garden is the formal Tudor feature of clipped hedges in knot patterns, and its own two words, read as a setter reads them, turn GARDEN into DANGER.

clue.text: Press that is keeping in check broadcasting tycoon?

parts.note: a mill is the press that crushes grain or olives

indicators.note: To keep a thing in check is to hold it in, so what is named next is written inside the letters already built.

parts.note: ie is the Latin id est, 'that is'
a station broadcasting is on air

explanation.surface: The newspapers keeping a broadcasting magnate under control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' is Fleet Street in the sentence and the grinding mill in the answer. The question mark is the setter conceding that plenty of people with a million own no business at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A tycoon is a magnate rich enough to throw weight about, and a millionaire has the money the title implies, which is what the question mark allows for.

clue.text: Solitary types intruded upon by fellow city dwellers

indicators.note: An intruder gets inside, so the word named next is written within the one before it.

parts.note: solitary types are loners
a don is a fellow of an Oxford or Cambridge college

explanation.surface: A college man barging in on people who would rather be left alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fellow' is the academic post rather than the ordinary chap the sentence offers: a don holds a fellowship at his college, and those three letters are the whole trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyone who lives in London is a Londoner, so the plural names the people of one particular city rather than town-dwellers at large.

clue.text: Where Turks might be slain — but not normally

indicators.note: What is not normal is abnormal, and letters set down abnormally are out of their proper order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A place where Turkish people might be killed, though not as a rule.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes 'slain' look like the end of a grim thought, and both halves of it are only letters. Nothing in the sentence says city: the definition is the four words in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Istanbul is Turkey's largest city, so it is one answer to where Turks might be, which is the work 'might' is doing.

clue.text: Facetious female's backchat mostly rubbish

parts.note: F is the usual abbreviation for female
lip is cheeky talk or backchat

indicators.note: most of the word is used, its last letter dropped

parts.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, something poor

explanation.walkthrough: In British slang 'pants' means rubbish; 'mostly' cuts it to PANT.
explanation.definitionFit: Flippant describes speech lacking proper seriousness, which is what a facetious remark shows.

clue.text: Carol fast approaching in SEAT

indicators.note: In puts the letters just named inside the word that follows it.

parts.note: what you do in a seat is sit; the capitals dress the word up as the Spanish car

something approaching is nigh

explanation.surface: A woman called Carol bearing down fast in her Seat.
explanation.walkthrough: The car marque is a costume: the capitals sell the Spanish make, and the word is there only for what a person does in one. 'Fast' is the Church's forty days, not speed.
explanation.definitionFit: Silent Night is the carol sung on Christmas Eve, Stille Nacht in the Austrian original, so the definition names it by its kind.

clue.text: Wood being crushed by stone instrument

indicators.note: What is crushed by something has that thing closing round it, so the word before goes inside the one after.

parts.note: st is the short form of the stone, the British fourteen-pound weight
pine is the wood

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stone' is the weight on the bathroom scales rather than the rock in the picture, which is where its two letters come from. A spinet is the small harpsichord of the seventeenth century, its strings plucked rather than struck.
explanation.definitionFit: A spinet is a compact keyboard instrument, a small harpsichord, so the definition is the musical sense of the word.

clue.text: Wind once again concerning with sharp blow

parts.note: re means concerning, as at the head of a memo
w is the standard short form of with
a rap is a sharp blow, as on a door

explanation.surface: The wind worrying everybody again with another sharp gale.
explanation.walkthrough: The wind of the sentence is the gale; the wind of the definition rhymes with find. Reading the first word the other way is the whole of the difficulty, and 'blow' is there to keep the weather going.
explanation.definitionFit: To rewrap is to wind the covering round something a second time, which is what winding it once again amounts to.

clue.text: Range of adult recordings

parts.note: A was the film certificate for adult
LPs are long-playing records

explanation.surface: A shop's range of records for grown-ups.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Range' is the selection on the shelf in the sentence and the mountains in the grid. The LP is the twelve-inch long-playing record, the album of the vinyl age.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alps are the mountain range curving through France, Switzerland and Austria, so the definition is the geographer's sense.

clue.text: Lame fox managed with reduced prey perhaps

prey cut smaller, its last letter gone, joins the fodder

clue.text: Giant going down when completely shorn

clue.text: Cultured dairy product mainly found on European island

clue.text: Dan Brown's first hit having shortage in stock

clue.text: Patron cross about new charges

the thoroughfare, shuffled

clue.text: Constantly inbound, regularly returning vessels

indicators.note: coming back, so the word is read in reverse

explanation.definitionFit: Nonstop as an adverb means without pausing, so continuously.
